strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing a real gap in user simulator research—existing simulators only model collaborative users, missing real-world complexity
Comprehensive framework with well-grounded categorization of four non-collaborative behaviors informed by marketing research and dialogue studies
Thorough experimental evaluation across two benchmarks with multiple models, revealing significant performance degradation (29.1% average drop for tangential behavior) and specific failure mechanisms
Detailed error analysis identifying root causes: helper API repetition for unavailable services, hallucinations for incomplete utterances, excessive apologies for impatience
Strong practical value with ready-to-use implementations on two benchmarks and extensible architecture for other domains
Fine-tuning experiments demonstrating vulnerability persists even with targeted training, revealing agents overestimate their robustness
Extensive documentation with all prompts, dialogue examples, and implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—non-collaborative behaviors are added through straightforward modifications (style transfer, goal augmentation, probabilistic triggers) rather than novel methods; core architecture heavily borrows from Yao et al. (2024) and baseline techniques from Luo et al. (2024), Laban et al. (2025)

Mixed and weak human evaluation results: simulator underperforms on tangential behavior, only achieves 60% win rate on combined behaviors, lacks inter-annotator agreement metrics, and doesn't strongly validate behavior realism
Incomplete utterance simulation relies on simple few-shot style transfer from LMSYS/WildChat with unclear representativeness; random truncation may not capture real user behavior complexity

Paper excels at diagnosis but provides minimal prescriptive guidance—no experiments on robustness mitigation (e.g., augmented training), no ablation studies on design choices (e.g., Prob+=0.1 escalation appears ad-hoc)
Goal alignment validation relies on GPT-4o-mini with potential bottleneck/bias; re-running failed dialogues could introduce gaming of metric; no analysis of overhead or failure frequency

Experimental limitations: selection of only 'book' tasks in MultiWOZ limits scope; 30-step limit is arbitrary; exclusion of human-transfer cases from τ-bench may miss failures; large baseline performance gap between benchmarks (45.5% vs 92.7%); no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Limited scope: restricted to task-oriented dialogue in booking domains; doesn't address other real-world complexities (typos, grammar errors, code-switching); behaviors somewhat artificial when injected via prompts

Weak baseline comparison—PBUS is relatively simple; missing comparisons with other possible approaches (RL-based simulators, adversarial training); no systematic exploration of why prompt-based approaches fail

strengths: Addresses an important, understudied problem: non-collaborative user behaviors in tool agent evaluation
Well-grounded taxonomy of 4 non-collaborative behaviors with support from marketing research and real-world data
Comprehensive multi-benchmark evaluation (MultiWOZ, τ-bench) with 5 baseline models and detailed failure mechanism analysis
Elegant technical approach: maintains goal alignment while simulating non-collaborative behaviors through dialogue state tracking and ending verification
Behavior-specific insights revealing model-dependent failure modes (hallucinations vs. duplicate API calls vs. over-apologizing)
Extensible framework demonstrated on multiple benchmarks showing generalizability
Exceptional reproducibility: complete prompts, implementation details, hyperparameters, extensive ablations and error breakdowns
Human evaluation (9 annotators) shows proposed approach generates more realistic non-collaborative behaviors than baseline (60% win rate)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing modules (dialogue state tracker, ending verifier) to existing simulator framework
Insufficient baselines: only compared against one prompt-based baseline; no comparison with other adversarial methods or human-generated dialogues
Narrow scope: only 4 behaviors with exclusion of others (toxic content, sarcasm, deception); human evaluation shows unnatural behavior combinations
No proposed solutions: paper demonstrates degradation but doesn't propose training strategies or defensive mechanisms to improve robustness
Small evaluation datasets: 89 MultiWOZ multi-domain scenarios, 157 τ-bench scenarios after filtering; arbitrary exclusions limit coverage
Methodological limitations: no statistical significance testing despite variability; GA metric relies on LLM-based regeneration that could bias toward easier cases
Limited real-world validation: behaviors grounded in literature but not validated against actual non-collaborative dialogues
Missing ablations: no analysis of prompt engineering choices, critical LLM modules, or sensitivity to hyperparameters
Presentation issues: 48 pages total with important details in appendices; dense figures and excessive dialogue examples

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: existing user simulators are agent-friendly but unrealistic for real-world deployment
Well-grounded taxonomy of non-collaborative behaviors informed by marketing research, dialogue studies, and real user data
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (GPT, Qwen, LLaMA) and benchmarks (MultiWOZ, τ-bench) with detailed failure analysis
Clever architecture that balances goal-aligned behavior with non-collaborative behavior simulation using dialogue state tracking and ending verification
Insightful finding that agents trained only on collaborative data become MORE vulnerable to non-collaborative behaviors
Practical and extensible framework demonstrated on additional benchmarks (ColBench, MINT)
Extensive documentation including all prompts, implementation details, and dialogue examples enabling reproducibility
Realistic scenarios testing multiple simultaneous non-collaborative behaviors
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily extends prior work (Yao et al. 2024) with straightforward augmentations (goal generation, style transfer, truncation, LLM-based checking)
Somewhat expected findings: that agents degrade under non-collaborative conditions is intuitive; limited guidance on architectural changes for robustness
Moderate human evaluation results: ~60% win rate only marginally better than chance; tangential behavior scores notably lower in combined settings
Incomplete behavior taxonomy: only 4 types; excluded toxic content; unnatural behavior combinations not fully addressed; unclear distinction from prior underspecification work
Test scenario selection concerns: MultiWOZ excludes retrieval tasks with weak justification (89 scenarios only); τ-bench excludes 8 human-transfer scenarios with observed excessive transfers
Goal alignment verification bias: regeneration until success could make problems appear easier; relies on GPT-4o-mini judge (MCC=0.77)
Limited baseline comparisons: only PBUS baseline; no adversarial dialogue approaches; no component ablations
Arbitrary experimental choices: 30-step limit validation indirect; only 4 trials per scenario; 50-step analysis shows inconsistent improvements
